1.note: Exod 27:17: the pillars are "banded" (חֲשֻׁקִים) with silver. The word plays on חֵשֶׁק, "desire". The same phrase comes back for Ibn al-Muʿallim.

2.note: 1 Kgs 7:46: Solomon cast the bronze vessels "in the plain of the Jordan, in the clay ground" (בְּמַעֲבֵה הָאֲדָמָה). Here "the heart" takes the place of the ground. The exact sense is uncertain.

3.note: Judg 3:22: the hilt of Ehud's sword went in after the blade. Here the carver comes in after the knife. לַהַב is both "blade" and "flame", so also "after the fire" of the roast.

4.note: In the Bible הֶאֱדִיב is "to grieve, make pine" (1 Sam 2:33). Possibly also a play on אָדֹם, "red": the fire browned them.

5.note: Literally "his ears". Onkelos renders עַל אֲזֵנֶךָ (Deut 23:14) as "on your weapon", and this is read so here.

6.note: Ruth 1:5. The names of Naomi's sons, Mahlon and Chilion, are the two words of the line before: מַחֲלוֹן "sickness" and כִּלָּיוֹן "failing". His eating put an end to both.

7.note: Literally "in the joined and the separated". Perhaps poems in rhyme against prose, or strophic poems against single verses. Uncertain.

8.note: Solomon ibn Gabirol, praised at length further on.

9.note: Joseph ibn Abitur, called Ibn Shatanash (Satanas).

10.note: Probably Moses ha-Kohen ibn Gikatilla (11th century). He is not named again in the survey below. Uncertain.

11.note: Probably Isaac ben Baruch ibn Albalia (11th century). The survey below calls him "the master Baruch". Uncertain.

12.note: Adonim was the Hebrew name of Dunash ben Labrat, but Dunash is named separately among the early poets. So perhaps another poet of this name. Uncertain.

13.note: The survey below has "Rabbi Joseph ibn Sheshet". Both names are kept as the edition prints them.

14.note: Isaac ben Reuben of Barcelona, author of azharot on the commandments (see below). עֲשׁוּקִים is usually "oppressed, robbed": perhaps poems taken by force from the heavenly host. Uncertain.

15.note: Not otherwise known. Perhaps a relative of the author.

16.note: Solomon ibn Gabirol, who signs his poems "Solomon ha-Katan" (the Small). The next lines play on קָטָן: יִקְטָן, Joktan, "the small one shall become a thousand".

17.he: וּפָשַׁט אֶת בְּגָדָיו וְלָבַשׁ בְּגָדִים אֲחֵרִים
17.note: Lev 6:4, the priest changing his garments. Isaac ibn Ezra is reported to have converted to Islam in Baghdad.

18.note: The son is Samuel ibn Abbas (al-Samawʾal al-Maghribi), who converted to Islam and wrote a polemic against Judaism. הִמְרִיץ is read from נִמְרָץ "grievous" (1 Kgs 2:8); the exact sense is uncertain.

19.note: 2 Sam 23:8, David's first hero, "Josheb-basshebeth a Taḥkemonite, that is Adino the Eznite". The title of the book comes from this verse.

20.note: Asaph, Jeduthun and the sons of Korah are the psalmists of the Psalter. סָף אָסָף is a sound play: "Asaph comes to an end" (סוּף).

21.note: Literally "the dwelling of his footstool" (הֲדֹם, Ps 110:1): where he lives. Uncertain.

22.note: Judg 4:11: Ḥeber the Kenite pitched his tent "at the oak of Zaanannim". So the verse gives away his name before the narrator says it.

23.note: תְּלִי is the celestial Dragon of medieval Hebrew astronomy (the constellation, or the nodes of the moon). In Gen 27:3 the word means "quiver".
